quality.question: My grey text on a white background looks faint, is that a problem?
quality.answer:
Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast) requires that meaningful visual cues (non-text UI components, icons, focus/selection indicators, graph lines, etc.) have at least a 3:1 contrast ratio against the background [1][2][5][3].

quality.question: buttons too small?
quality.answer:
Level AA — SC 2.5.8 (Target Size (Minimum)): pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when Spacing, Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, or Essential exceptions apply [5][4].  
Level AAA — SC 2.5.5 (Target Size (Enhanced)): pointer targets must be at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels, except when Equivalent, Inline, User Agent Control, or Essential exceptions apply [1][2].  
Therefore, buttons smaller than 24×24 fail Level AA unless an exception applies; buttons between 24×24 and 44×44 meet Level AA but not Level AAA (for example, links inline in text do not need to meet the 24×24 requirement) [5][1][3].

quality.question: What contrast do large text and icons need?
quality.answer:
Level AA — SC 1.4.3: large-scale (large) text must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. [2][5]

Level AA — SC 1.4.11: icons (graphical objects and user interface components) must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors. [3][4]

Level AAA — SC 1.4.6: normal text requires 7:1 contrast, and large-scale text requires at least 4.5:1. [1]

Exceptions (no contrast requirement) include incidental text, pure decoration, text not visible to anyone, text in pictures with significant other visual content, inactive UI components, and logotypes. [2][1][5]

quality.question: What's the difference between 1.4.3 and 1.4.6?
quality.answer:
SC 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum) — Level AA — requires text and images of text to have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, with exceptions (large-scale text/images: at least 3:1; incidental or decorative text, text not visible to anyone, text that is part of a picture with significant other visual content, and logotypes have no contrast requirement) [1].  
SC 1.4.6 (Contrast Enhanced) — Level AAA — is an enhanced (stricter) contrast requirement (Level AAA) that uses the defined contrast/relative‑luminance formula and related notes (including conversion to linear RGB and consideration of ambient light) and has Test Rules for checking enhanced contrast [2][4].  
In short: 1.4.3 is the Level AA minimum contrast requirement; 1.4.6 is the Level AAA enhanced/stricter contrast requirement and should be tested using the 1.4.6 formula/notes and Test Rules [1][2][4].

quality.question: Does disabled button text need good contrast?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast): UI components and their states must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent colors, except for inactive components or where the user agent determines appearance [1]. Inactive (disabled) user interface components are not required to meet the 1.4.11 contrast requirement — they are exempt from this non-text contrast rule [2]. Note: 1.4.11 addresses non-text contrast for components; text contrast is covered by other criteria (e.g., 1.4.3), see related techniques [5].

quality.question: Does a logo need to meet contrast rules?
quality.answer:
Level AA — SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum): text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement [3].  
Level AA — SC 1.4.11 Non‑text Contrast: user interface components and graphical objects (parts of graphics required to understand the content) must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1; the WCAG text for 1.4.11 does not explicitly list logos as an exemption [1].  
Level AAA — SC 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced): text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement [5].

quality.question: Which success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2?
quality.answer:
The following success criteria are new in WCAG 2.2. [2]

Level AA: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) [2]; 2.5.7 Dragging Movements [2]; 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) [2]; 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) [2].

Level A: 3.2.6 Consistent Help [2]; 3.3.7 Redundant Entry [2]. Level AAA: 2.4.12 Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) [2]; 2.4.13 Focus Appearance [2]; 3.3.9 Accessible Authentication (Enhanced) [2].

quality.question: Is 4.1.1 Parsing still required?
quality.answer:
No — Success Criterion 4.1.1 Parsing (Level A) was removed from WCAG 2.2 and is obsolete, so it is not required for WCAG 2.2 conformance. [1][4]

However, authors required by policy to conform to WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 may still need to test and report 4.1.1, and many issues that would have failed 4.1.1 are now addressed by other criteria (for example Info and Relationships or Name, Role, Value). [2][4]

Technique G134 is an example technique related to 4.1.1, but techniques are informative examples and not mandatory requirements. [3]

quality.question: At what width must content reflow without horizontal scrolling?
quality.answer: Level AA — Success Criterion 1.4.10 (Reflow) requires vertical-scrolling content to reflow without horizontal scrolling at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels. [1][3] 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels at 400% zoom (test by setting the viewport to 1280px wide and zooming to 400%). [1][2][3]

quality.question: How many times per second can content flash?
quality.answer:
Level A — Success Criterion 2.3.1 (Three Flashes or Below Threshold): content must not exceed the flash thresholds that trigger seizures; failures involve 3.5 flashes or more within one second, so authors must avoid 3.5 flashes/second or greater [4][5].  
Level AAA — Success Criterion 2.3.2 (Three Flashes): do not flash content more than 3 times a second [1].  
Technique G19 recommends ensuring no component flashes more than three times in any 1‑second period (a stricter, easier-to-test approach that meets Level A) [5][2].

quality.question: Can I use a puzzle CAPTCHA on my login page?
quality.answer:
You may use a puzzle CAPTCHA on your login page, but to meet WCAG 2.2 Level A (Success Criterion 1.1.1 Non-text Content) you must provide text alternatives that identify and describe the CAPTCHA’s purpose and provide alternative CAPTCHA forms using output modes for different types of sensory perception to accommodate different disabilities [2][3][5].  
Use Technique G143: include a text alternative that identifies the content as a CAPTCHA, describes the type of task, and, when an alternate version exists, instructs how to find it [1][4].  
Also ensure the page contains another CAPTCHA serving the same purpose using a different modality (Technique G144); G143 and G144 together are sufficient to meet SC 1.1.1 for CAPTCHAs [4][5].

quality.question: Quel est le contraste minimum pour le texte ?
quality.answer:
Au niveau AA (SC 1.4.3), le contraste minimum est de 4,5:1 pour le texte normal et de 3:1 pour le texte grand (Large Text) [2].  
Les exemptions — texte accessoire/incidental, pure décoration, non visible, partie d’une image contenant d’autres contenus visuels significatifs, et logotypes — n’ont pas d’exigence de contraste [2].  
Au niveau AAA (SC 1.4.6), le contraste minimum est de 7:1 pour le texte normal et de 4,5:1 pour le texte grand [1].  
Le texte est considéré comme « grand » s’il fait au moins 18 points non gras ou 14 points gras [3].
